definition: Response selection is the executive-control process of choosing the appropriate action or response, especially when there is conflict between competing responses. In this source, it is described as a stage of performance that can be helped by novelty, particularly under more difficult task conditions.

reasons: The packet supports that novelty can enhance response selection, especially under more difficult task conditions, but it does not define response selection as an executive-control process of choosing the appropriate action, nor as a general conflict-resolution concept.
“Stage of performance” is not supported by the packet’s wording; the source only reports an effect on response selection in a specific task context.

The packet does not explicitly define “response selection” as an “executive-control process of choosing the appropriate action or response”; it instead describes “conflict-related response selection,” “executive control,” and “response selection” in relation to novelty and task difficulty without stating that specific definition.

While the packet mentions novelty facilitating conflict resolution and discusses “conflict-related response selection and inhibition,” the definition’s framing (“especially when there is conflict between competing responses”) is only indirectly supported via the use of the Simon task and discussion of conflict resolution, not stated as part of a direct definitional explanation.
